title: Alzheimer's risk gene APOE4 may have a reversible weakness
summary:
Mount Sinai researchers have uncovered new details about how APOE4, the strongest known genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, may contribute to brain damage. Two studies published in Cell and Cell Stem Cell show that the gene can damage blood vessels in the brain and encourage the accumulation of abnormal proteins associated with neurodegenerative disease. The findings point to disease processes that may be reversible and highlight a new human brain tissue platform derived from stem cells that could speed up the search for treatments.

Alzheimer's disease gradually damages memory, thinking and behavior, and affects more than 7 million older adults in the United States. Researchers have known for years that blood vessels in the brain deteriorate as Alzheimer's progresses, especially in people who carry APOE4. What has been less clear is why this happens and whether the vascular damage contributes directly to the disease. Damage to the brain's circulation has often been treated as a consequence of Alzheimer's rather than as a process that could help drive it.

For the Cell study published on September 24, the scientists combined existing datasets to build a single cell transcriptomic atlas of blood vessels in the human brain. The map showed patterns of gene activity across the different cells that create and support the brain's vascular system. The team found that APOE4 altered the behavior of pericytes, cells that normally help stabilize small blood vessels and support the blood brain barrier. In the presence of APOE4, the pericytes changed into myofibroblast-like cells that produce scar tissue. That promoted vascular fibrosis and increased the buildup of amyloid around blood vessels, which could interfere with blood flow.

The researchers also found evidence that this process could be reversed. Blocking TGF-β signaling, which plays a role in communication between cells and in tissue remodeling, restored pericyte coverage while reducing fibrosis and amyloid around blood vessels. The result was reproduced in aged APOE4 mice.

"Damage to the brain's blood vessels is not simply a late consequence of Alzheimer's disease; it is a biologically active process caused by APOE4 that may be reversible," said corresponding author Joel W. Blanchard of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. "These findings reveal new therapeutic targets for preserving vascular function and limiting amyloid accumulation."

A major part of the research relied on miBrains, three dimensional human brain tissue developed by the Mount Sinai team from induced pluripotent stem cells. miBrains include all of the major cell types in the human brain, including neurons, supporting glial cells, myelin producing cells, and cells that make up blood vessels.

In the Cell Stem Cell study, miBrains carrying APOE4 developed higher amounts of abnormal alpha-synuclein, a protein most strongly associated with Lewy body dementia and Parkinson's disease. The experiments revealed that APOE4 causes cholesterol to accumulate inside astrocytes, support cells that perform several essential functions in maintaining brain health.
why_it_matters: The studies suggest blood-vessel damage may help drive Alzheimer's instead of only following it. If that is confirmed, it could point scientists toward new treatments, though the reversal was shown in mice and lab-grown tissue.

questions.question: How was damage to the brain's circulation often treated before?
options: As the main cause of every single case of Alzheimer's
As something that only ever affects people who are young
As a consequence of Alzheimer's rather than a process that could help drive it
As a harmless change that came along with normal aging
questions.correct_answer: As a consequence of Alzheimer's rather than a process that could help drive it

questions.question: What did the single cell atlas show?
options: How many people in the whole country carry the APOE4 gene
Patterns of gene activity across the cells that create and support brain blood vessels
Which foods change gene activity in the human brain
The exact age at which each person gets Alzheimer's disease
questions.correct_answer: Patterns of gene activity across the cells that create and support brain blood vessels

questions.question: What did pericytes change into in the presence of APOE4?
options: Cells that clean up amyloid around vessels
Neurons that store memories for a long time
Stem cells that repair the damaged vessels
Myofibroblast-like cells that produce scar tissue

options: Reduced fibrosis and amyloid after blocking TGF-β signaling
The buildup of cholesterol in the blood
The loss of all of the pericytes
The growth of several new brain regions
